place: Stanbury is a small grey stone village strung along the Keepers' Way, quiet and a little sleepy, with lichen on the walls and thin smoke from a few tired chimneys. By the road stands the old keepers' shelter, a low stone hut with deep eaves, a stout door and a cold hearth, where keepers once slept on their way to Wardlow; set along its sunny wall at a child's height is a row of flat carved stones, each with a name, a lantern and the mistake that keeper got up from, and over the door the biggest stone of all. Every scene at the wall happens in daylight, with warm stone and bees in the ivy until Thursday's cold rain, and it feels like a kitchen wall where a family marks how tall everyone has grown: old, kind and lived-in, never a graveyard, with Wardlow standing dark far off to the west.

hosts.name: Hild (with Dun), Ch 45 only
hosts.voice: Few words, slow and plain, and she lets silences sit. She comes through the thinning rain on foot beside Dun. Her teaching lines are only questions (proposed for Ch 45: "Why carve the fall, and not just the carrying?"). She may tell her own story because it is hers to tell, in short plain sentences, never more than three at once, with no self-pity and no speech: "A keeper carves the flame in when the work is handed on." "Mine never was." She owns her part without asking for comfort, never asks the children to carry the fire for her, never tells them what to do next, and never foretells anything. She understands Ember, and she sits by the shelter door that night. Dun says nothing and stands out of the rain under the eaves.

hosts.name: The Keepers' Stones (not a host: carved words, Ch 41 to 45)
hosts.voice: The stones never speak, glow or move; they are only read. Each was carved by a young keeper about themselves, in first person, in short plain lines of 12 words or fewer, spelled the modern way with old-shaped, worn letters: a name, a little lantern, what went wrong, and how they got up (proposed shape: "I dropped the fire in the snow. I walked home for more."). Never sad words, dates, "here lies", "in memory" or anyone lost. The biggest stone, over the door, carries the canon line word for word: "A light that's taken will not catch. A light that's given will." These carvings are ideal "Your line" reading for the eldest-slot reader.

modeled_behavior: When you want to give up, say "I did it before. I can do it again," and try once more.
echo_plan: Ch 41, Odyssey 11 (those who came before): the travelers go to hear from the keepers who went before, but they hear them only by reading a sunny wall; no dead, no ghosts, no voices, no underworld, no offering, and every stone was carved by a young keeper about their own first carrying. Ch 42, Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 1 (thanks to those who taught him): proposed, when [[child:eldest]] reads [[pro:eldest.pos]] first whole line he says "Thank you" to the keeper who carved it, and the flame stands a little taller, as a thank-you always makes it (canon world rule). Ch 43, the stories of those who came before: [[child:middle]] reads the picture story of the keeper who dropped the fire in the snow and walked all the way home for more; it quietly rhymes with Part 7's wind, but nobody says so and nobody brings up the knots. Ch 44, Odysseus weeps, then goes on: [[child:youngest]]'s tears are allowed, never praised away ("she didn't cry" is never written), and she gets up by helping Ember. Ch 45, Tiresias tells the way home, turned: Hild tells the truth about the past, not the future; no prophecy, no instructions, and her honesty is the gift. It stays quiet because story text never names Homer, Marcus Aurelius or the Bible, the stones teach nothing, and nobody explains what the wall means; only the Sunday plan's grown-up note may name the sources. Faith (toggle on): blessing key Proverbs 24:16 only; a grown-up faith note may mention Peter, who wept and was welcomed back at a breakfast by the sea (John 21), for Hild's confession. Nothing in the story depends on it.

tuesday_pair.too_little: [[child:eldest]] gets the old letters wrong again and again, says "It's stupid" about the letters (never about a person), and nearly quits (falling apart). He is likable and never laughed at, and he gets up in the same chapter: "I read hard words before. I can do it again," a lantern breath, "Oops… up again!" with the crouch and spring, then sound by sound.
tuesday_pair.too_much: [[child:middle]] guesses wildly (proposed: "It says SAUSAGES!", which delights Ember) and says "Doesn't matter what it says" (shrugging it off: carelessness, not too much bouncing back). The laugh is with him, never at him. He changes in the same chapter by reading the pictures carefully while [[child:eldest]] reads the letters, and on Wednesday his careful reading of the pictures turns out right.

set_piece: Tracing the carved letters with a finger, sound by sound. At breakfast a grown-up writes a short word big (on paper, in a tray of flour or on a steamy window), and each child runs a finger along each letter, saying its sound, then says the whole word. The youngest traces the first letter of their own name and says its sound. When a letter comes out wrong: "Oops… up again!", crouch down small and spring up with arms wide, and trace it again.
clue: Ch 45: Hild's stone, the last in the row and greened over with moss, so nobody reads it before Friday. [[child:eldest]] finds it: her name, HILD, the mistake she got up from as a girl, and a lantern carved with no flame in it yet. "A keeper carves the flame in when the work is handed on," she says. "Mine never was." The reveal: she was the last keeper, and the beacon went out on her watch because everyone thought someone else would go.
friday_question: Why do you think the keepers carved their mistakes on their stones?

trial.title: The Keepers' Stones

bands.3-4: Draw one thing you're proud you did on your own keeper's stone (a stone shape cut from paper, or a big flat stone), and tell a grown-up about it.
bands.5-6: Tell three hard things you have done before, starting each one with "I did it before…". Then draw one of them on your stone.
bands.7-9: Ask [[gp:real]] about a time they got it wrong and got up again (in person or on the phone), then tell it back in three sentences. Draw it on your stone and write a few words under it, like a keeper.

trial.safety_line: Grown-ups: use a paper stone, or a stone too big to swallow (bigger than a toilet-roll tube is wide), with washable paint, and stay beside little ones while they paint.

i_can.Little: I can say how I feel and take a lantern breath with a grown-up, then try again.
i_can.Middle: I can say "Oops, I can fix it," and fix it myself, without being told, even when I'm cross.
i_can.Big: I can get it wrong in front of others, calm myself without blaming anyone, and try again.
i_can.Stretch: I can help someone else get back up, and laugh at my own mistakes.

in_real_life: In real life, only grown-ups carry a flame.
In real life, foxes don't talk, and we never touch or cuddle a wild animal; we watch it from far off with our grown-up.
In real life, we never stay out or sleep somewhere new without our grown-up.
In real life, we tell our grown-ups about every new friend, and a good friend never asks us to keep a secret from them.
flags_for_jon: No Part 8 sheet was available at drafting time (parts are drafted in parallel), so continuity came from the canon's Part 8 rows; it has now been checked against the Part 8 sheet. Ch 41 opens with Grandma's reply to the Ch 40 letter sent from Edith's roof, then "Last time…" carries Part 8's Start Again trial as a story memory. Ch 40's hook ("Hild carried fire up Wardlow? Then why didn't she say?") is answered in Ch 45, not on Monday. The Monday reply must not hint at Hild's secret, which Grandma knows and keeps ("That's not mine to tell"). No other part sends home "homesick" or "proud".

The canon gives Stanbury no host for Monday to Thursday, and the kit asks for hosts. Proposed detail inside the beats, with no new grown-ups: the children sleep in the keepers' shelter, which by the old law of the Keepers' Way is kept for anyone carrying the Keepers' Lantern, and they eat from a basket Edith packed (bread, cheese, apples and a rind for Ember). On Friday Hild sits by the shelter door, so the shelter counts as a roof with a host: Ember carries the Ch 45 letter, and Ch 46 opens with the reply. Stanbury is the only village on the road that the canon gives no light to, and it is not in Ch 54's crowd; this sheet adds no flame-sharing there. Say if you want one.

"Always seen in daylight" (canon gazetteer) is read as: every scene at the wall happens by day, Thursday's rain is daytime rain, and night appears only as the closing sleep indoors (Ch 45's "That night they sleep in the keepers' shelter"). Wardlow "far off" and dark is seen at dusk from the shelter door.

Turn child this part: Alfie (the bible §5 order Hugh, Clara, Alfie, itself flagged). In Ch 44, which Clara leads, Ember says the "if" half of his Middle plan ("If I mess something up…"), the reader pauses, and Alfie says "then I say 'Oops, I can fix it' and fix one part." Proposed moment inside the canon's "Each child shows how they get back up": in the dash out of the rain his backpack tips and his odd treasures roll into the wet grass, and he fixes it himself. It must not take Clara's key act (wrapping Ember in the fleece).

Ch 43's "remember when" is from Ch 34, and the canon doesn't say whose moment it is. It must never hand back Hugh's knots (a mistake; strengths rule 14). Proposed: Ember hands Alfie back his own "What else could we try?" on the hill above home, which leads him to read the pictures when the letters are too hard. Alternative: Clara's "West," as she took Hugh's hand.

Hild's Ch 45 question is not in the canon. Proposed: "Why carve the fall, and not just the carrying?", which the Friday Pause & ask builds on. Avoid "What would you carve on yours?": it invites a child to bring back a mistake already owned (Hugh's knots, Alfie's giggle).

Hild's girlhood mistake on her stone is not given in the canon. Proposed carving: "I said someone else would carry it. Then I got up and went." It quietly sets up her confession (everyone thought someone else would go) without explaining it. Keep it small, true and not frightening.

Keepers and carriers: the canon says each keeper carved a stone after their first carrying, and Grandma and Edith both carried fire up Wardlow as girls, so they might have stones. The canon is silent. This sheet proposes the drafts show neither: a stone reading [[gp:name]] would need grandparent blocks, a Nan version and a remembered version, and the lantern's base is already where Grandma's name lives. Clara's Ch 41 stone "with a little lantern exactly like theirs" is just a carving of the Keepers' Lantern (ring handle, horn windows, little chimney). Your call.

New names: the canon names no keeper but Hild. The sheet proposes that 1d reads other keepers' stories without reading their names (the pictures and the "I" lines carry them), so nothing needs a name check. Any named old keeper would need a true Old English root, canon §2's naming rules and the formal Tolkien and real-place check, and must not look like Edith, Osric, Aldwin or Hild's fallback, Wynn.

Guard rails for drafting and pictures. The stones are flat, square stones set in a sunny shelter wall at child height, carved by living young keepers about themselves: never upright slabs in grass, never headstones, dates, "here lies" or "in memory". Tolkien images to avoid: no runes (the letters are ordinary letters, old-shaped and worn), no tomb, no door that opens to a spoken or read word, and no voices from stone. In pictures the carvings are marks, with the readable line printed beside them (kit open item 3); access versions read the letters by touch (bible §6).

Strength boundary: "When you want to give up" can read as Keep Going. Drafts should use the modeled line just after getting it wrong (Hugh's wrong readings, Clara's tears), per strengths' "Which strength is it?" (a hard thing before anything has gone wrong is Keep Going). Canon §1 lists "sticking with the hard old letters" under Hugh's Keep Going; the tag stays `Bounce Back · between falling apart and shrugging it off` as the canon sets it. Ch 42's canon line "I read hard words before. I can do it again" is kept word for word; the fridge card uses the modeled behavior's wording. "Oops… up again!" and the crouch-and-spring (Clara: spring up with arms wide) still appear in every chapter.

Trial: the canon wording is kept, with pronouns made neutral ("you") so the card suits any child. The 7-9 task uses [[gp:real]], so a family with Nan or a remembered grandparent gets "a grown-up who loves you", and "in person or on the phone" is added. The kit says trials are "doable at home with nothing special", but this one needs a grandparent; the canon wins. "Draw one of them on your stone" (5-6) and "Draw it on your stone" (7-9) are added so every band makes a stone, as the title says. The safety line covers paint and stones for little ones. No play-it version, because no task needs a real incident. The canon's table is unchanged.

Week words: "homesick" (Clara in Ch 44, and the pull of home when the stones speak of walking home) and "proud" (the Little trial, and keepers proud of getting up). Use "proud" only about a deed ("proud of getting up"), never as praise of who a child is, and never as the too-much fault. Both need two uses in one chapter and one more in the part (1d).

"In real life" lines: the flame and the talking friend are on bible §5's list, and the friend line (the sentence every part shares) was added in the continuity pass, since Ember talks all week; "touch or cuddle a wild animal" covers Clara wrapping Ember in Ch 44 and Ember sleeping round her; "sleep somewhere new without our grown-up" covers four nights in a roadside shelter with no grown-up, a production call beyond bible §5's four motifs (like kit open item 20). Together they are about 70 words, too long for the dinner card's 50-word limit (kit 13.1). Suggested: the Sunday plan carries all four and the dinner card the flame and fox lines.

Timeline, set in the continuity pass (the Part 10 and Part 11 sheets agree; please confirm). Ch 45 is "six nights before the longest night". The walk from Stanbury to Oxley at the foot of Wardlow ("far off") takes the two days between Ch 45 and Ch 46, off the page, with the children housed at farm doors on the Keepers' Way by its old law; Ch 46 is the third day, Ch 47 and 48 the fourth, Ch 49 and 50 the fifth, and Ch 51 sets off before dawn on the sixth, the longest night itself. Ch 44 uses "the last of Wistan's fleece", and no chapter between Ch 23 and Ch 44 uses up the rest. Blessing key for the week: Proverbs 24:16.
